title: Working with dates

cells.text: Back to the deliveries. Dates let you see trends over time, like which month was busiest. First the dates must be real dates, not text, using `pd.to_datetime()` from Lesson 16.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load the deliveries and turn order_date into real dates.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv")
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"])
df.head()

cells.text: Real dates have a **.dt** toolbox, just like text has .str. `.dt.year` gives the year, `.dt.month` gives the month as a number from 1 to 12, `.dt.day` gives the day of the month, and `.dt.day_name()` gives the weekday, like Monday.

cells.prompt: Press Run to see the month of every order.
The orders run from January to early April. How many different months do they cover? Pick one, then press Run.
Replace ___ so the new month column holds each order's month number, then press Run.
hints: It's the .dt part that gives 1 to 12. No brackets after it.

cells.prompt: Your turn: show only the orders placed in March (month 3). Filter on the month column.
Count the orders in each month, using groupby on the month column. Count the order_id column.

cells.text: `day_name()` is the one .dt action that needs brackets, because it works out a name rather than reading a number.

cells.prompt: Last one: add a day column with each order's weekday name, then show the customer and day columns.
hints: Line 1: df["day"] = df["order_date"].dt.day_name(). Line 2: pick the 2 columns.

recap: After pd.to_datetime(), the .dt toolbox gives year, month, day and day_name(). Use them to filter or group by time.
